data.title: Japanese Yen a Key Beneficiary of AI-Related Risk Aversion — Market Talk
data.description: The Japanese yen is best positioned to benefit from risk aversion stemming from concerns over the sustainability of lofty valuations in artificial-intelligence stocks, MUFG Bank's Derek Halpenny says in a note. data.title: Eurozone Wage Growth Accelerates, But Remains Modest — Update
data.description:
By Paul Hannon

Eurozone wage growth accelerated slightly in the three months through September, but remained modest despite the pickup in inflation triggered by the war between the U.S. and Iran.

The European Central Bank on Friday said wages negotiated by labor unions and similar groups were 2.57% higher in the third quarter than a year earlier, an increase in the annual rate of growth from 2.45% in the three months through June.

Since the start of the war, officials at the ECB have highlighted the outcome of wage negotiations as a key indicator as to whether the jump in energy prices triggered by the conflict is set to keep inflation above their 2% target.

But there are few signs as yet that workers are securing larger pay rises to cover increased energy bills.

"What we don't see at the moment is second-round effects, not yet," Bank of France Governor Emmanuel Moulin said in an interview with CNBC on Thursday. "We need to be vigilant about what will happen and that's the reason we've increased rates in the past."

The ECB raised its key rate in September and June.

The eurozone's annual rate of inflation rose to 4% in October from 1.9% in February, the month in which the war began.

That pickup in the pace of price rises has weakened the spending power of eurozone households, and for the year as a whole the European Commission now estimates that wages adjusted for inflation will increase by just 0.4%, a sharp slowdown from 1.8% in 2025.

It expects real wages to rise at a similarly slow pace next year, with the commission forecasting that compensation per worker will rise at an unchanged pace of 3.5%.

Write to Paul Hannon at paul.hannon@wsj.com

data.title: Wall St futures slip as Anthropic debut fails to reassure AI investors
data.description:
Key points:
  • Futures down: Dow 0.2%, S&P 500 0.76%, Nasdaq 1.63%
  • Anthropic down 6.5% a day after its debut
  • Gap gains on Old Navy recovery

US stock futures fell on Friday as Anthropic shares retreated after a blockbuster debut, dashing hopes that the high-profile listing could steady an AI trade rattled by growth and valuation concerns, while hawkish signals from Federal Reserve officials this week also weighed on sentiment.

Anthropic shares slid 6.8% in premarket trading after surging more than 17% on Thursday in their highly anticipated market debut. The stock began trading more than 34% above its offer price of $83.

The Claude chatbot creator's IPO was seen as a key test of investor confidence in the AI theme after a bruising few weeks for the sector. Concerns over potentially slower data center expansion, higher borrowing costs and the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have intensified fears about returns on massive spending.

The Nasdaq was 13.6% below its record closing high of October 6.

Among hyperscalers, Amazon , Meta , and Microsoft declined more than 1.8% each, while Alphabet was muted. Amazon and Alphabet are among Anthropic's biggest investors.

Chipmakers were lower, with Nvidia down 2.6%, while Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Marvell , and Micron lost between 3.5% and 5.5%.

Neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius also dropped more than 5% each.

Data center stocks IREN , Applied Digital and Core Scientific fell between 2.8% and 4%.

At 4:57 a.m. ET, Dow E-minis (YMcv1) were down 99 points, or 0.2%, and S&P 500 E-minis were down 54.5 points, or 0.76%. Nasdaq 100 E-minis were down 434 points, or 1.63%.

Wall Street's main indexes were on track for their steepest weekly decline since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced Liberation Day tariffs.

The selloff in AI-linked stocks has largely overshadowed a strong earnings season.

Of the 462 companies in the S&P 500 to have reported results through Wednesday, 83.5% reported earnings above analyst expectations, according to an analysis from Tajinder Dhillon, head of earnings and equity research at LSEG Data and Analytics.

INFLATION, FED IN FOCUS

Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Anna Paulson said on Thursday the Fed will need to raise interest rates again because inflation is too high, while arguing that shared understanding matters more than explicit guidance on the rate outlook.

Markets are pricing in a 98.4% chance of an interest rate hike from the central bank at its next meeting in December, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.

Next week's personal consumption expenditures (PCE) figures will provide further clarity on the Fed's monetary policy path after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report last week.

Brent crude prices fell 1.6% and were heading for a third straight weekly loss on expectations of a supply surplus, with crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz returning to roughly prewar levels.

Markets were also assessing the outcome of the meeting between Trump and his Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, after the leaders issued a joint peace declaration that made no mention of the conflict between the US and Iran.

Among other movers, apparel retailer Gap rose 2.5% after its Old Navy brand posted better-than-expected quarterly sales.

data.title: India’s top philanthropists donate ₹11,554 crore in FY26, 11% more than in the previous year
data.description:
A total of 219 philanthropists donated ₹11,554 crore in the financial year ending March 2026, an 11 per cent increase from ₹10,380 crore the previous year, according to the EdelGive Hurun India Philanthropy List 2026 released on November 20 in Mumbai.

Shiv Nadar and his family retained the top position for the fifth consecutive year, donating ₹2,593 crore, roughly ₹7.1 crore per day, through the Shiv Nadar Foundation, primarily toward Arts, Culture & Heritage and Education. Gautam Adani and family more than doubled their giving to ₹877 crore, a 127 per cent jump, climbing three places to second. The Bajaj family held third place with ₹632 crore, while Mukesh Ambani and family ranked fourth with ₹620 crore.

The top 10 collectively contributed ₹6,572 crore, accounting for 57 per cent of total donations. Ranjan Pai and family were new entrants to the top 10, ranking ninth with ₹219 crore. Rohini Nilekani ranked tenth with ₹215 crore and remains the most generous woman on the list. Women’s representation grew to 29 from 24 the previous year.

New entrants to the list nearly quadrupled, rising from 12 to 45, contributing a combined ₹696 crore. Raamdeo Agrawal and Motilal Oswal, co-founders of Motilal Oswal Financial Services, led new entrants with ₹120 crore and ₹119 crore, respectively. N. R. Narayana Murthy joined the list this year, bringing combined Infosys co-founder family giving to ₹920 crore.

Education remained the dominant cause, receiving ₹4,188 crore or 36 per cent of total donations, funded by 200 of the 219 philanthropists. Healthcare donations rose sharply by 82 per cent to ₹1,768 crore. Environment and Sustainability grew 86 per cent to ₹813 crore.

Self-made philanthropists numbered 125, or 57 per cent of the list, and accounted for 65 per cent of all donations. Mumbai led by number of philanthropists with 64, while New Delhi led by value at ₹3,168 crore. The list was published jointly by EdelGive Foundation and Hurun India for the 13th consecutive year.

data.title: Beijing to bar young 'red-chip' firms from listing outside mainland China, sources say
data.description:
Key points:
  • Red-chip firms must redomicile in China before they can list offshore, sources say
  • Red-chip firms are registered abroad but control assets and businesses in China
  • Beijing has been gradually tightening oversight of capital raising by red-chip firms

China's securities watchdog has told some law firms it will not approve plans by red-chip firms to list outside mainland China, people familiar with the matter said, a move that tightens its control of capital raised offshore and could dent Hong Kong's IPO market.

Red-chip companies are registered abroad, mainly in tax havens, but control assets and businesses in China via equity ownership or contractual agreements.

The structure is favoured by Chinese startups, particularly tech firms, keen to raise capital in places like Hong Kong or New York to take advantage of more relaxed rules and deeper pools of funds available from foreign investors.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has told law firm representatives in recent days that red-chip companies established after the introduction of new offshore listing rules in 2023 must be re-domiciled in China before they can list offshore, said the people.

The people declined to be identified as the regulatory guidance was confidential. The move is being reported for the first time by Reuters.

China and the US are competing fiercely to gain the upper hand in tech, particularly in AI and semiconductors, which has led to efforts by Chinese authorities to sharpen their scrutiny of technology, data and capital going outside its borders.

The CSRC did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Oversight of red-chip firms has gradually become stricter.

Prior to March 2023, Chinese companies employing overseas holding structures to raise capital abroad did not need regulatory approval. That changed with the advent of the new rules.

Then this year, the CSRC told Reuters in March that it was examining the "necessity and compliance" of red-chip structures, particularly those formed after March 2023.

Despite that warning, some red-chip IPO hopefuls and their advisors have been seeking approval to list outside the mainland without dismantling their existing structure and shifting their domicile back to China, one of the people said.

Most of those applicants failed to convince the regulator that a red-chip structure was necessary, prompting the tougher stance, the person added.

HONG KONG IPO MARKET COULD BE HURT

A drop-off in listings from red-chip firms is likely to hurt but not hobble Hong Kong, the top IPO destination for Chinese firms, which has seen business boom for the past 18 months.

Funds raised via IPOs in Hong Kong during the first 10 months of this year surged 84% from the same period last year to hit HK$404 billion ($52 billion), though the CSRC has slowed approvals of IPOs since September.

In addition to going slow on approvals for listings by AI, chip and humanoid robot firms after a market frenzy in those sectors, it has more broadly increased its scrutiny as markets have weakened.

Last year, one-fifth of 131 Hong Kong listings approved by the CSRC involved offshore holdings, the majority of which used a red-chip structure, according to Chinese law firm Han Kun.

So far this year, the CSRC has approved Hong Kong listings for just 6 red-chip companies, a sharp decline from 50 approved last year, according to data compiled by law firms and Reuters.

There were nearly 600 listing applications pending in Hong Kong at the end of October, official data showed.

Most of them are mainland Chinese firms though it was not clear how many are red chips given that the number includes applications that were filed confidentially.

There are, however, at least four active Hong Kong IPO applicants which have an offshore holding company structure for their mainland China businesses, according to a Reuters review of filings with the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Any red-chip firms seeking to list in Hong Kong or New York could now face a long wait before coming to market due to the time and costs involved in becoming incorporated in China.

But some, like Chinese AI firm StepFun, have been working on shifting their domicile back to China to pave the way for a planned overseas listing, sources have said. StepFun did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Asked about news of the ban on red-chip firms listing outside mainland China, the Hong Kong bourse said it "welcomes issuers with a range of ownership structures, provided they meet all applicable regulatory requirements in Hong Kong and other relevant jurisdictions."

($1 = 7.8410 Hong Kong dollars)

data.title: Why Is AMD Down 5% In Premarket Today?
data.description:
Key points:
  • AMD stock shed 7.7% the previous day after Hunterbrook said the chipmaker’s China exposure makes it vulnerable and took a short position.
  • AMD said it remains in compliance with U.S. laws.
  • CNBC’s Jim Cramer called the short seller report a ‘hitjob.’

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) fell more than 5% in early premarket trading on Friday, extending a selloff after reports questioned its ties to China even as the chipmaker said it remains in compliance with U.S. laws.

“AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” a company spokesperson told Bloomberg. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”

Hunterbrook Media, affiliated with Hunterbrook Capital, said in a report on Thursday that AMD’s exposure to the Chinese market leaves it vulnerable to more U.S. chip export restrictions.

Hunterbrook Capital simultaneously disclosed a short position in AMD stock, which fell 7.7% on Thursday.

The issue came close on the heels of the crisis at Nvidia, whose CEO Jensen Huang was booted out after his disclosure of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Since last week, the U.S. has announced new restrictions on advanced AI technology for Chinese end users and is investigating Huang’s dealings and risk exposure.

Analysts See Little Merit In AMD Allegations

“We believe the shortseller's attack on AMD does not hold up to close scrutiny,” CNBC analyst Jim Cramer said on X.

“I agree with AMD when it says ‘the claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships…’ We would buy it if we could for the trust.”

In a follow-on post, he called the short seller report a “hitjob.” He wrote, “At one point the author says he doesn't even know if any of what's he's charging AMD with is wrong! But this is such a crummy tape...nothing you can do other than buy some when you can, like we will for my charitable trust, and thank the shortseller for a discount back to where it was before that amazing quarter.”

The Futurum Group Daniel Newman called the report “an opportunistic move when the market and the AI trade is most fragile.”

“Market wants any reason to sell. Shorts can have a field day with this. But that doesn't make these reports accurate whatsoever,” he said on X.

Retail View On AMD

On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for AMD remained ‘bullish’ for a second day on Friday. “$AMD Clear manipulation to bring this down but it’s so strong,” said a trader.

Another wrote: “$AMD Hunterbrook has a financial incentive to push a bearish narrative. Allegations aren’t proof of wrongdoing. AMD’s long term AI growth story remains compelling and I’m not letting short seller headlines shake my conviction.”

As of the last close, AMD stock is up 128% year to date.

data.title: Colder weather expectation lifts week-ahead prices
data.description:
European week-ahead power prices rose in early Friday trading as colder weather is expected across central western Europe and wind power supplies are also expected to drop.

  • The German week-ahead baseload contract (TRDEBWKD1) rose 6.5% to €237 ($260.20) per megawatt-hour at 0955 GMT, LSEG data showed.

  • The equivalent French contract (TRFRBWKD1) rose 9.2% to €224.9/MWh, according to LSEG data.

  • A colder spell is set to deepen into early next week, with anomalies falling to 6 degrees Celsius below seasonal norms in Germany and similar in the Netherlands by Tuesday, while France stays near normal, EnergyScan analysts said.

  • Wind speeds are also expected to stay low on average in Germany, France and Spain, they added.

  • German wind power output was expected to fall by 5.9 gigawatts on Monday to 13.1 GW, LSEG data showed.

  • Demand in Germany was expected to rise by 1.5 GW to 61.1 GW on Monday, as average temperatures drop nearly 6 C to 0.5 C, the data showed.

  • French nuclear availability fell 2 percentage points to 78% of total capacity.

  • French wind supply was seen down 9.1 GW at 5.1 GW while demand is expected up 3 GW on colder temperatures, LSEG data showed.

  • On the forward side, the German year-ahead baseload contract (TRDEBYc1) rose 0.7% to €142.50/MWh, tracking higher gas costs, the data showed.

  • The equivalent French contract (TRFRBYc1) was untraded after closing at €111.35/MWh, LSEG data showed.

  • The European carbon market's benchmark contract was down 1% to €81.19 a metric ton.

($1 = 0.9108 euros)
